raw_response.country: United Kingdom (England and Wales, with brief comparison to Scotland)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines domestic household water and sewerage service access in England and Wales, focusing on affordability, water poverty, utility disconnection for non-payment, and self-disconnection.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, it examines legal, regulatory, and administrative governance of domestic water provision and social security policy. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing household access and continuity: privatisation and OFWAT RPI+K price-cap regulation, volumetric metering and tariff rules (including the Water Industries Act 1991 prohibition on rateable values after 2000), DSS direct-payment eligibility and deduction priority rules under the Social Security Regulations 1987 (including the 'six month rule'), Licence Condition H County Court debt-recovery and disconnection procedures, and prepayment metering. Because the paper fails Criterion 3 (no empirical evidence, E05), both decision and plain_criterion2_decision are exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Narrative social policy overview and research-agenda essay ('A review of issues for research') structured around a conceptual heuristic framework (Figure 1). Although it cites secondary statistics, regulatory documents, and previously published surveys to illustrate policy debates, it reports no primary data collection, no original quantitative or qualitative empirical analysis, and no systematic empirical synthesis methodology. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses access-relevant outcomes from secondary reports and official OFWAT statistics, including household water bill affordability, arrears/debt, domestic water supply disconnections, and self-disconnection under prepayment devices, though without original empirical measurement.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the article is a non-empirical narrative policy review and research agenda rather than an empirical study or systematic review, there is no identifiable empirical study design, analytical sample, or primary exposure-outcome analysis.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English in the Journal of Social Policy.

evidence_quotes.quote: Figure 1 shows how three levels of debate can be distinguished in a heuristic model on which to base plans for research.

Although the model gives a simplified picture of the issues involved, it provides a framework within which to review the water poverty debate in the three areas of increasing charges, ability to pay, and debt and disconnection.

Adjudication officers are responsible for decisions about making direct payments under the Social Security Regulations 1987 and can do so for most claimants already in debt for water bills. But rules governing access are complex.

The Licence places a legal requirement on companies to seek recovery of debts in the County Court before disconnection, to afford customers 'the protection of County Court scrutiny of their circumstances' (DOE briefing note for Licence Condition H).
Yet the annual number of disconnections has increased from 8,426 in 1989-90 to 18,636 in 1992-3, following a peak in 1991-2 of 21,282.

Nevertheless, water and sewerage services do not come free of charge and a key role of future social policy research should be to explain and comprehend the factors leading to increases in bills, to develop ideas for preventing the burden of these increases from falling disproportionately on the poor, and to continue to evaluate methods for alleviating the problems of people for whom water poverty has become a very real issue.

raw_response.exposure: Water industry privatisation, OFWAT RPI+K price-cap regulation, metering and tariff rules, DSS direct-payment eligibility rules, and Licence Condition H debt-recovery and disconnection procedures (reviewed narratively)
raw_response.outcome: Household water affordability, water bill debt, domestic supply disconnection, and self-disconnection (secondary figures reviewed narratively)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Domestic water customers and low-income households in England and Wales (general policy discussion citing secondary sources; no primary study sample)
raw_response.rationale: Full text matches record metadata (Huby 1995, Journal of Social Policy). Although the paper directly addresses household water affordability and disconnection (c1, c4) and concrete legal/administrative rule-type mechanisms governing service continuity—such as OFWAT tariff/metering rules, DSS direct-payment eligibility rules, and Licence Condition H County Court disconnection procedures (satisfying both plain and narrow readings of c2)—it is a narrative social policy review and research-agenda essay with no primary data, no original empirical analysis, and no systematic review method (c3 = no, c5 = no). Excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence).
raw_response.study_design: Narrative policy review and research agenda (non-empirical)
